finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the attacker-supplied token with loose == against the stored token. If the stored token is a numeric string of the form 0e<digits>, any other 0e<digits> value (e.g. "0" or "0e1") compares equal, letting an attacker reset the password without knowing the token.

finding.guards_checked: $row truthiness only rejects missing rows; $db->quote() protects SQL text not the comparison; no type check or hash_equals in this function (strict sibling at line 14 avoids this)

verdict.guard_found: none. $row truthiness (reset.php:4) only rejects a missing row. $db->quote() (reset.php:3, 5-6) protects the SQL text, not the comparison. Nothing in reset_password_loose uses hash_equals or a type check. The strict sibling reset_password uses hash_equals at reset.php:14, but the candidate's sink is the loose function.
verdict.reason: At reset.php:4, `$row['token'] == $token` is a loose comparison with no guard, so when the stored token is a PHP numeric string (e.g. "0e..."), an attacker-supplied "0" compares equal and the password is replaced at reset.php:5-6. The attacker only needs to be able to call the reset function with the victim's email, which is the anonymous-reset case; the caller is not in the directory, so reachability is assumed. The exploit is conditional on the stored token's format: random hex tokens almost never match that pattern, so practical likelihood is low, but the defect is real and the candidate states that condition.

finding.claim: Both reset functions accept an empty submitted token when the stored token is empty or NULL: PHP null == "" is true, and hash_equals("", "") is true. A resets row with an empty/NULL token lets an attacker reset that email's password with token "".
finding.source: reset.php:2 and :12 $token (attacker can submit empty string)

verdict.guard_found: Only `$row` truthiness (reset.php:4 and :14). No rejection of an empty submitted token, no `token <> ''` or `IS NOT NULL` filter in the SELECT (reset.php:3, :13). No control blocks an empty match.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: PHP `null == ""` is true at reset.php:4, and `hash_equals(null→"", "")` is true at reset.php:14, so an empty stored or NULL token with an empty submitted token would pass both functions and reach the UPDATE at reset.php:5-6 and :15-16. Whether such a `resets` row can exist, and which endpoint passes an attacker-controlled `$token`, depends on the schema and the insert and request-handling code, which are not in this directory (the only file present is reset.php), so exploitability cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: Reset tokens are never invalidated: the success path updates the password but never deletes or marks the resets row used, and the lookup has no expiry predicate and no ORDER BY. A previously issued token can be replayed indefinitely, and with multiple rows per email the checked token is arbitrary.

finding.guards_checked: No DELETE or UPDATE on resets in this file; no expiry check in the query. A sweeper or other module elsewhere may expire tokens; not visible here

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:3 and :13 select the token with no created_at/used predicate and no ORDER BY. reset.php:4 uses loose == and :14 uses hash_equals, but neither is an expiry or single-use control. reset.php:7 and :17 return true without deleting or marking the resets row. The only file in the directory is reset.php, so no sweeper or other invalidation exists in the code available.
verdict.reason: At reset.php:7 and reset.php:17 a successful reset returns true without deleting or marking the resets row, and the lookups at reset.php:3 and :13 have no expiry or used predicate, so a previously issued token still matches and can be replayed. The attacker needs to have held that token earlier (anonymous, but requiring a prior token), so this is a real replay weakness rather than an unauthenticated takeover; the "arbitrary row" wording is slightly loose but does not change the verdict.

finding.claim: Neither reset function limits token guess attempts: there is no counter, lockout or rate limit, so the token can be brute-forced if its entropy is low. Low severity and depends on upstream throttling and token length, which are not visible here.
